blocks.md: **When Danish firms offshore more — import more materials, for reasons driven by world supply — they employ fewer workers and shift toward high-skilled ones. When they export more, driven by world demand, they grow on every margin.**

- Effects of firm-level offshoring (imports of materials) and exporting on workers' wages, employment and firm outcomes.
- Population of Danish workers matched to the universe of private-sector Danish firms, plus product-level trade flows by origin and destination country ([Danish Matched Worker-Firm Data](note:danish-matched-worker-firm-data)).

Firm-time outcomes are regressed on $\log X_{ft}$ (exports) and $\log M_{ft}$ (offshoring/imports). OLS is biased because firm-time productivity sits in the residual and productive firms both import and export more. Firm fixed effects remove permanent productivity ([Fixed Effects Regression](note:fixed-effects-regression)); time-varying productivity needs instruments:

- **Imports**: world export supply, $WES_{jt} = \sum_{ck} s_{jck}\,WES_{ckt}$ — each country $c$'s supply of product $k$ to the world (excluding Denmark), weighted by the firm's initial share of $ck$ in its materials imports.
- **Exports**: world import demand, $WIS_{jt} = \sum_{ck} s_{jck}\,WID_{ckt}$ — each country's imports of product $k$ from the world (excluding Denmark), weighted by the firm's initial export shares.

blocks.md: Columns: (1) all firm-years; (2)–(3) firms that offshore at some point; (4)–(5) firms that both offshore and export, using predicted values of both.

- **OLS vs IV**: OLS says offshorers are bigger in every way — selection on productivity. Instrumented, offshoring *reduces* employment.
- **Skill composition**: instrumented offshoring raises the high-skilled share, i.e. reduces the low-skilled share — offshoring substitutes for low-skill work.
- **Exports are different**: all outcomes rise with instrumented exports.
